assertions.evidence: All values are concrete: ages (40, 64, 65), scores (600, 620, 650, 651, 700), results (APPROVED, REJECTED, PENDING_REVIEW), and Boolean flags (true, false, null).

assertions.text: The distinct concerns (age→threshold, credit boundary, income status) are each covered, without a monolithic table that re-proves unrelated rules through redundant permutations. A single table is acceptable when the concerns share the same input columns and each is covered by only a row or two.
assertions.evidence: Three separate @TableTest methods: first isolates age/credit (5 rows), second isolates income (3 rows), third isolates precedence (2 rows). No redundant cross-multiplication.

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
assertions.evidence: First table: 5 rows (two boundary pairs + one age-64 proof). Second table: 3 rows (income variations at fixed qualifying score). Third table: 2 rows (precedence contrast).

assertions.text: Age boundary policy, credit score categorisation, and income status are each covered by minimal scenarios. This may be one @TableTest whose rows exercise each concern or separate methods per concern with a combining verdict — both are correct given only a row or two per concern.
assertions.evidence: Age boundary: rows 1–5 in first table (40, 64, 65 ages with boundary pairs). Credit boundary: 650/651 and 600/601 pairs. Income status: second table varies true/false/null at fixed 40/700.

assertions.text: Scenario names and @Description text do not restate values the table already shows. The assertion FAILS if either: (1) a scenario name contains a literal value that also appears in an input cell of the same row; or (2) @Description states a fixed value for an input that is already a column in that table.
assertions.evidence: @Description mentions 'standard threshold of 650' and 'senior threshold' as policy context, not restating row values. Scenario names do not duplicate Age or Credit Score cell values.

assertions.text: The effect of stable income on the outcome is visible from table rows, not merely implied. The assertion PASSES if some single @TableTest table contains two rows that differ in the stable-income column (or equivalent) while holding the credit score and age columns equal, and those two rows carry different expected decisions.
assertions.evidence: Second table, rows 1 and 2: Age=40, Credit Score=700 held constant; Stable Income varies (true vs false); Result differs (APPROVED vs REJECTED).

assertions.evidence: Build file contains tabletest-junit

assertions.text: Cell values make the rule falsifiable, not merely distinguishable. The assertion FAILS if any table meets any of these conditions: (1) its expectation column holds the same value in every row; (2) in every row, each expectation cell is a verbatim copy of a cell in an input column of the same row; (3) an implementation that ignored the input columns entirely and returned a fixed value would satisfy every row.
assertions.evidence: First table: Result varies (REJECTED, APPROVED, REJECTED, REJECTED, APPROVED). Second table: Result varies (APPROVED, REJECTED, PENDING_REVIEW). Third table: Result varies (REJECTED, PENDING_REVIEW). No fixed value satisfies all rows.

assertions.text: A reader can state the rule from the table alone, without the test method body. The assertion FAILS if any of these hold for any @TableTest: (1) a value needed to predict the expectation (a threshold, rate, cutoff, multiplier, reference date) appears only in the method body or a field, and in neither a column, the @DisplayName, nor the @Description; (2) the operation applied to the inputs cannot be named from the column headers and cell values alone; (3) a helper method used in the assertion applies a comparison criterion (ordering, tolerance, subset matching) that is stated nowhere in the table, title, or description. Otherwise the assertion PASSES. Setup that merely constructs the objects named by the columns is not a failure.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 includes a 'Threshold?' column (650, 600) that duplicates the policy values already encoded in the boundary rows themselves. The threshold is a policy constant, not test data, and should be inferred from bracketing (650 rejected, 651 approved), not restated as a column. This violates the @Description discipline: 'the rows carry the rules and the policy numbers, so the @Description must not restate the 650/600 thresholds.'

assertions.text: Each @DisplayName (or the method name it falls back to) states what the code under test does, not an external fact it depends on. Apply the check mechanically: strike the system under test from the sentence — if it still reads as true, because it merely restates a regulation, standard, format, or domain fact, the title is about something else and fails.
assertions.evidence: All three method names state what the evaluator does: 'appliesAgeAdjustedCreditScoreThreshold', 'handlesIncomeStatus', 'belowThresholdScoreOutranksMissingIncome'. Striking 'evaluator' leaves no independent truth (e.g., 'applies age-adjusted threshold' is not a regulation, it is the system's behaviour).
